topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to focus on public health faculty development; findings may not generalise broadly to other sectors or non-academic settings without additional evidence on implementation contexts.
takeaways: Faculty resistance to AI integration is addressable through structured development programs; design interventions that move staff from skepticism to practical readiness rather than assuming resistance is fixed.

Position faculty/staff development as the critical lever for embedding AI literacy in organisations — this suggests investing in train-the-trainer and peer-learning models before rolling out AI tools organisation-wide.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on middle school education frameworks, likely applicable to secondary education contexts globally, but implementation would need adaptation for different curricula and regional education systems.
takeaways: AI literacy for younger learners benefits from integration into broader digital literacy rather than taught in isolation — this suggests how to structure AI capability development across educational pathways.

A holistic framework approach (combining technical skills, critical thinking, and ethics) is more effective than standalone AI modules — consider how this model might apply to adult professional AI capability building in your organisation.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focused on European public health context; competencies identified may differ from other sectors or regions with different healthcare systems and digital maturity levels.
takeaways: Identify which digital competencies from the framework are most critical for your team's current role and prioritise upskilling in those areas first, rather than attempting comprehensive training across all domains.

Use the framework's competency domains as a structure for mapping skills gaps in your workforce and designing targeted development programmes tailored to public health or similar regulated environments.
Consider how the framework's European context (regulation, healthcare infrastructure, policy) translates to the Australian healthcare setting before directly adopting recommendations.

articles.title: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Upskilling and reskilling priorities for the gen AI era  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Broad applicability across sectors, though based on McKinsey's client base and may reflect developed-economy perspectives more heavily than emerging markets.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation are most exposed to AI displacement and prioritise upskilling interventions for those cohorts first, rather than attempting organisation-wide reskilling simultaneously.
Design reskilling programmes around emerging roles (e.g. prompt engineering, AI governance, human-AI collaboration) rather than assuming employees can simply transition to unrelated fields.

Embed AI literacy fundamentals (how gen AI works, its limitations, responsible use) into existing training pathways so employees build capability incrementally rather than treating it as a separate initiative.

articles.title: Development and influencing factors of artificial intelligence literacy and computational thinking in Chinese university students - Nature
articles.snippet: Development and influencing factors of artificial intelligence literacy and computational thinking in Chinese university students  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to Chinese university context — findings on curriculum structure, educational policy, and student demographics may not transfer directly to Australian higher education systems, which have different AI integration approaches and student populations.
takeaways: Identify which factors most strongly predict AI literacy development in your student or employee cohort (e.g. prior technical exposure, domain-specific training, mindset) and prioritise those in capability-building programs.

Map computational thinking skills alongside AI literacy as separate but complementary competencies — teaching one does not automatically build the other, so design training to address both explicitly.

Consider whether your organisation's approach to AI literacy accounts for individual differences in prior knowledge and learning pathways, or if it assumes a one-size-fits-all model that may leave gaps.

articles.title: Fostering AI literacy in pre-service teachers: impact of a training intervention on awareness, attitude and trust in AI - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Fostering AI literacy in pre-service teachers: impact of a training intervention on awareness, attitude and trust in AI  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses specifically on pre-service teachers; findings may not generalise to established educators or other professional groups. Geographic scope unclear from title and snippet.
takeaways: Structured training interventions can measurably improve educators' awareness and trust in AI systems — consider implementing similar modules in your organisation's teacher onboarding or professional development programs.
Attitude shifts toward AI among educators require active intervention rather than passive exposure; design training to address misconceptions and build confidence, not just convey information.

Pre-service teacher populations may represent a more receptive audience for AI literacy than established teachers with entrenched practices — if targeting educators, prioritise early-career cohorts for maximum impact.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title and snippet alone. Appears to explore organisational mechanisms, likely applicable across sectors, but geographic scope and sample composition are unclear.
takeaways: AI adoption in organisations can have contradictory effects on creativity — understanding both positive and negative mechanisms helps leaders design implementation strategies that maximise creative benefits while mitigating risks.

When rolling out AI tools, explicitly assess how they might constrain employee thinking or autonomy (the 'double-edged' risk) alongside efficiency gains, and design governance to protect space for novel problem-solving.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — appears to be empirical research but geographic scope and sample characteristics cannot be determined from the title and snippet provided.
takeaways: Psychological ownership of work (the sense that employees 'own' their role or projects) may be a key lever for encouraging employees to actively shape and customize AI tools to fit their needs, rather than passively accepting AI systems as imposed.

Paternalistic leadership styles (benevolent, authority-based) may create conditions where employees feel safe experimenting with AI customization; consider whether your leadership approach enables or inhibits this kind of exploratory AI adoption.

AI crafting — the active modification and tailoring of AI tools by end users — appears to be a mechanism linking psychological ownership to collaboration; organizations should clarify which aspects of AI systems employees can safely modify and encourage this hands-on experimentation.

articles.title: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Corporate sustainability and artificial intelligence-enabled workforce transformation: a dual-pathway model of employee capability, empowerment, anxiety, and job insecurity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample composition not evident from title/snippet. The dual-pathway model may apply broadly to organisations undergoing AI transformation, but geographic scope, sector diversity, and sample size are unclear. Findings should be validated across different organisational contexts and geographies before assuming universal applicability.
takeaways: When implementing AI-enabled transformation, design interventions that simultaneously build employee capability and foster empowerment — the 'dual-pathway' framing suggests these are complementary levers for reducing anxiety and job insecurity rather than addressing anxiety alone.

Assess and monitor both rational concerns (job insecurity driven by capability gaps) and emotional concerns (anxiety about change) separately during AI rollout; one-size-fits-all change communication may miss employees experiencing different psychological pathways.

Use AI transformation as an opportunity to clarify career pathways and reskilling support upfront — the model implies that capability development and genuine empowerment (autonomy, involvement in decisions) are more protective against demoralisation than reassurance alone.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — without access to full article, geographic scope and sample characteristics are unclear. Findings on job crafting responses to AI adoption may vary by industry, organizational context, and cultural factors.
takeaways: Monitor whether employees respond to AI adoption by actively reshaping their roles (approach) or withdrawing from tasks (avoidance) — understanding this distinction helps tailor change management strategies to support productive adaptation rather than disengagement.

Design AI implementation to clarify how employees can repurpose their skills and create meaningful work beyond automation, as this directly influences whether they view AI as an opportunity to craft better roles or a threat to avoid.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study's sample composition, which is not evident from the title and snippet. The findings on AI adoption, psychological safety, and ethical leadership may apply across sectors, but geographic scope and sample characteristics require review of the full paper.
takeaways: Monitor psychological safety when rolling out AI tools — employees who feel unsafe speaking up about AI-related concerns are at higher risk of depression and reduced wellbeing.
Ethical leadership during AI adoption is protective: leaders who model ethical AI use and create space for values-based discussion can buffer against negative mental health outcomes.
Assess your current culture before AI implementation — if psychological safety is low, address that foundation first, and ensure leaders actively champion ethical AI practices during the transition.

articles.title: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Unlocking human potential in the AI Age: how employee-AI collaboration transforms work engagement through dual psychological pathways  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title and snippet alone. The theoretical framework on psychological pathways may apply broadly across sectors, but findings would need to be validated across different organisational contexts, cultures, and AI implementation stages.
takeaways: Employee-AI collaboration can drive engagement through distinct psychological mechanisms — understanding which pathways matter most (e.g., autonomy, competence, social contribution) helps you design collaboration workflows and support strategies tailored to your team's needs.

Use this framework to diagnose engagement challenges in AI-enabled roles: if engagement is low, assess whether barriers stem from psychological needs (skill gaps, loss of control, social disconnection) and target interventions accordingly.

Design onboarding and change management to explicitly address both psychological pathways — e.g., ensure AI tools enhance rather than replace judgment, and maintain peer collaboration and meaning-making opportunities alongside automation.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner insights are likely based on client engagements across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample composition and methodological details are not transparent from the title and snippet alone.
takeaways: Shift from 'AI adoption' framing to 'AI adaptation' — focus change management on building new human behaviours and mindsets rather than just implementing technology.
Design change interventions that explicitly target the behaviours employees need to work effectively with AI, not just tool rollout and training.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on study design and sample characteristics not evident from title/snippet. The approach-avoidance framework may apply across sectors, but geographic scope and sample size are unclear.
takeaways: When introducing AI tools, anticipate that employees will adopt either approach behaviours (engaging with upskilling) or avoidance behaviours (withdrawing from tasks) — proactive communication about AI's role and support for skill development can shift employees toward approach-focused job crafting.

Design onboarding and change management to address psychological distance and threat perceptions; employees who perceive AI as complementary rather than threatening are more likely to actively reshape their roles rather than retreat from them.

Monitor for divergent job crafting responses post-AI adoption — some staff may expand responsibilities while others contract them; targeted coaching and peer learning opportunities can help avoiders reframe AI as a tool to enhance rather than replace their work.

articles.title: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: AI Transformation Is a Workforce Transformation  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG analysis likely draws on consulting engagements across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample composition, methodological rigor, and geographic weighting are unclear from the snippet alone.
takeaways: Frame AI adoption as a workforce capability challenge, not just a technology implementation; design change management interventions that address employee skill gaps, role redefinition, and career anxiety alongside technical rollout.

Conduct a workforce readiness audit before major AI deployments to identify which teams, functions, or demographics will face the steepest capability gaps—use this to prioritise upskilling, redeployment, or support intensity.

Embed behaviour change principles (e.g., clear communication of benefits, early wins, peer champions) into your AI transformation roadmap to increase employee buy-in and reduce resistance during the transition.

articles.title: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Redefine AI upskilling as a change imperative  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — based on McKinsey's consulting experience across sectors, but specific case studies and client contexts are not detailed in the snippet provided, limiting assessment of applicability to different organisational types or geographies.
takeaways: Frame AI upskilling not as a technical training initiative but as an organisational change programme — this positioning helps secure leadership buy-in and allocate appropriate change management resources.
Treat AI capability development as a strategic imperative alongside business transformation, not a standalone HR or IT project, to ensure sustained commitment and cross-functional participation.

Design upskilling interventions with explicit attention to managing employee resistance and identity shifts, since AI adoption often requires people to rethink their roles and value in the organisation.

articles.title: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI Is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be a Stanford GSB perspective piece without specified research methodology, sample, or geographic scope. Insights may reflect Silicon Valley/US tech sector viewpoint rather than broader workforce contexts.
takeaways: Identify which roles in your organisation are most exposed to AI disruption, then design targeted upskilling programs for those teams rather than attempting organisation-wide AI literacy initiatives.

Create explicit conversations with employees about how AI will augment (not replace) their work, focusing on concrete examples of new tasks and responsibilities they'll take on as routine work is automated.

articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature

takeaways: When rolling out AI tools, prioritise establishing psychological safety first — employees who feel unsafe to voice concerns about AI are at higher risk of depression and disengagement.

Ethical leadership during AI adoption is not optional; leaders must actively model and communicate ethical AI use to prevent negative mental health outcomes and reduce employee anxiety about technological change.
Assess your organisation's current psychological safety climate before major AI implementation; this is a critical intervention point to protect employee wellbeing during the transition.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: The science of why friendships keep us healthy - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: The science of why friendships keep us healthy  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Moderate — APA literature reviews synthesise research across studies but may have a US academic bias in sourced literature.
takeaways: Strong friendships appear to reduce mortality risk as much as quitting smoking and exceed the protective effects of exercise and weight loss — a striking equaliser that shows social connection rivals major health interventions.
The health boost from friendships works through multiple pathways: reduced stress hormones, better immune function, and improved mental health, making it a uniquely comprehensive health intervention.
Loneliness activates the same threat-detection systems as physical danger, suggesting our brains treat social isolation as a genuine survival risk — which is why it feels so acutely uncomfortable.

articles.title: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized - Science Daily
articles.snippet: Your personality may be more genetic than scientists realized  Science Daily
articles.generalisability: Unable to assess from snippet alone — headline claims about genetic influence on personality require examination of underlying research methodology, sample size, and study design to determine applicability.
takeaways: The finding challenges the long-held assumption that personality is primarily shaped by environment and upbringing — suggesting nature may play a larger role than the nurture-focused psychology of recent decades suggested.

If personality traits are more heritable than previously thought, it has counterintuitive implications: people may have less flexibility to 'reinvent' themselves through willpower alone, yet understanding genetic predispositions could help people work *with* their natural tendencies rather than against them.
This kind of nature–nurture reframing tends to spark fierce debate among scientists and the public — making it a fascinating window into how we update our understanding of what makes us 'us.'

articles.title: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Musical preferences unite personalities across the globe  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Likely high — Cambridge research on global music preferences suggests findings apply across diverse cultures, though specific sample composition and size would need verification.
takeaways: Your taste in music might say more about your personality than you think — people with similar personalities gravitateto similar genres worldwide, suggesting music preferences are a universal window into how people tick.
The finding challenges the idea that music taste is purely cultural or regional; instead, personality appears to be a common thread linking what we listen to across continents and cultures.
This is counterintuitive because we often assume music preferences are shaped by local culture and trends, yet personality seems to create a baseline that transcends geography.

articles.title: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026 - Wiley & Sons
articles.snippet: Out of the dark – Psychological perspectives on people's fascination with true crime - Perchtold‐Stefan - 2026  Wiley & Sons
articles.generalisability: Moderate — a psychological literature review on true crime fascination likely draws from international research, but specific geographic coverage and sample characteristics are not evident from the title and snippet provided.
takeaways: True crime appeals to a fundamental human curiosity about risk and transgression — we're drawn to understanding 'the dark' from a safe distance, which taps into cognitive and emotional needs.
The psychological reasons people binge true crime content may include a sense of control (following a solved case) and pattern-recognition practice — making it more than just entertainment.

Understanding why we're captivated by true crime reveals something counterintuitive: exposure to danger narratives can feel reassuring rather than purely threatening, depending on how the story unfolds.

articles.title: How dogs think - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: How dogs think  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: Moderate — synthesises existing research on canine cognition, but scope and specific studies reviewed are unclear from the snippet alone.
takeaways: Dogs' cognitive abilities are more sophisticated than often assumed, with documented capacities for memory, emotional recognition, and social reasoning — not just stimulus-response machines.
The gap between human and canine cognition is smaller in some domains (social learning, emotional responsiveness) than we might intuitively expect.
Understanding how dogs actually think challenges popular assumptions about intelligence and reveals surprising parallels to human social and emotional processing.

articles.title: Personality traits linked to differences in brain structure - University of Cambridge
articles.snippet: Personality traits linked to differences in brain structure  University of Cambridge
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on sample size and demographic composition, which are not detailed in the snippet provided. Brain imaging studies typically have moderate sample sizes and may skew toward WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) populations.
takeaways: Your personality isn't just psychological—it's literally reflected in the physical structure of your brain, challenging the idea that personality and biology are separate domains.
This finding suggests why personality is relatively stable across time: the brain structures associated with traits are anatomically embedded, not just behavioural habits.
The link between brain structure and personality opens fascinating questions about causation: does your brain shape your personality, or do your life choices reshape your brain?

topics.label: Psychological Safety

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2026  PwC
articles.generalisability: High — large-scale global survey capturing workforce sentiment across multiple countries and sectors, though representativeness depends on PwC's sampling methodology and respondent demographics.
takeaways: Identify specific psychological safety concerns your workforce shares with global peers by reviewing which 'fears' resonate most locally — this can inform targeted interventions and communication strategies.
Use global trend data on worker 'hopes' to benchmark your organisation's culture against peers and identify gaps in how well you're meeting employee needs for belonging and autonomy.

Consider how geopolitical and economic uncertainties affect psychological safety perceptions in your team — survey insights may reveal which external factors are driving disengagement or anxiety that affect speaking up.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study's sample size and organisational context — details are unclear from the title and snippet alone. The finding that AI adoption can negatively impact employee mental health via reduced psychological safety is likely relevant across sectors, but effectiveness of ethical leadership as a mediator may vary by organisational culture and implementation approach.
takeaways: AI adoption initiatives that bypass psychological safety — where employees fear speaking up about concerns, mistakes, or ethical issues — may increase depression and disengagement; proactively build trust and invite employee input during AI rollout.

Ethical leadership is not optional during AI adoption; leaders who model ethical decision-making and hold AI use accountable to values appear to buffer negative mental health effects and strengthen psychological safety.

Screen for depression and mental health impacts in employees during and after AI implementation, particularly among those with lower baseline psychological safety or who report ethical concerns about AI systems.

articles.title: Team Dynamics Weaken When Employees Turn to AI Instead of Colleagues - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: Team Dynamics Weaken When Employees Turn to AI Instead of Colleagues  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Limited — appears to be conceptual analysis rather than empirical research. Generalisability depends on underlying evidence not evident from title/snippet; likely reflects Western corporate contexts but specific geographic scope unclear.
takeaways: Monitor whether AI adoption is reducing face-to-face collaboration and peer knowledge-sharing in your teams — create norms that preserve direct colleague interaction even when AI tools are available.

Consider designing AI implementation guidelines that encourage employees to consult colleagues first for complex problems, using AI as a supplement rather than a replacement for team communication and relationship-building.

Actively reinforce psychological safety by discussing how AI tool use might affect team cohesion, and create space for teams to decide when collaboration with colleagues should take priority over individual AI-assisted problem-solving.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG's analysis likely draws on consulting experience across multiple sectors and geographies, but specific sample composition, size, and methodology are not detailed in the snippet provided.
takeaways: Creating psychological safety reduces barriers for underrepresented groups to contribute equally, suggesting it's a lever for both inclusion and team performance rather than separate initiatives.
Leaders should assess whether team members feel safe speaking up without fear of embarrassment or retaliation — this foundation enables broader participation and reduces 'silent' knowledge loss.

articles.title: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024 - American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.snippet: Psychological safety in the changing workplace: Work in America 2024  American Psychological Association (APA)
articles.generalisability: US-focused findings on workplace psychological safety trends. While psychological safety principles are universal, this report reflects American workplace contexts, labour practices, and employee demographics that may not directly transfer to Australian organisations.
takeaways: Identify specific barriers to psychological safety in your team (e.g., fear of speaking up, blame culture) by conducting a brief pulse survey or focus group aligned with APA's 2024 framework—this baseline helps you track progress.

Create one concrete 'speak-up' mechanism (e.g., anonymous feedback channel, regular team reflection time, or blameless post-mortems) and measure uptake and feedback quality over 3 months to build trust incrementally.

Examine your organisation's response to mistakes and dissent—leaders who visibly acknowledge their own errors and act on critical feedback set the tone for psychological safety more than any policy document.

articles.title: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential - McKinsey & Company
articles.snippet: Superagency in the workplace: Empowering people to unlock AI’s full potential  McKinsey & Company
articles.generalisability: Moderate — McKinsey research typically draws on global consulting experience and surveys, but findings are most directly applicable to large, well-resourced organisations. Specific implementation approaches may vary significantly across different organisational contexts, sectors, and geographies.
takeaways: Psychological safety is foundational to 'superagency' — employees need to feel trusted and supported to experiment with AI tools without fear of failure or judgment, which requires explicit leadership messaging and permission to learn.

Empowering people requires clarifying role boundaries and decision-making authority in an AI-augmented environment; without this clarity, employees may hesitate to act or over-defer to AI recommendations.

Practical support mechanisms (training, safe experimentation spaces, feedback loops) are essential — psychological safety alone is insufficient; people need concrete tools, time, and permission to build AI capabilities.
